Measured tradeoffs

Random input at 2,097,152 keys: geometric repair used 1.197 rotations/key and 1.999 random bits/key; treap used 2.001 rotations/key and 32.000 random bits/key. Their final heights were 43 and 51 edges, with mean node depths 23.139 and 25.853, respectively.

Converging input at 2,097,152 keys: geometric repair used 1.724 rotations/key and 2.001 random bits/key; treap used 2.001 rotations/key and 32.000 random bits/key. Their final heights were 115 and 50 edges, with mean node depths 34.337 and 25.391, respectively.

Comparison at the largest common size: 2,097,152

Averages are over completed trials; ± one standard error when repeats exist. Python random streams are paired across strategies; C++ uses a different PRNG. Maximum final height is the largest final node depth observed across those trials, not height averaged across seeds or time. Larger partially completed groups are excluded.

How large did each implementation reach?

Trials advance through increasing sizes. Direct resource failures and probes stopped at a shared pipeline boundary are distinguished below. These are resource-limited measurements of these implementations and validators, not algorithmic size limits.

Python boundary: After every implementation/input pair completed 2,097,152 keys, a 4,194,304-key probe hit the 768 MiB cap inside the common BST validator (seen.add(id(node))). The main required validation allocations at that size are estimated at 816 MiB, before interpreter overhead. Remaining higher-size probes were cancelled or not launched to avoid repeating this shared validation-memory bottleneck.

Method and interpretation

  • Measured implementations are the current Python geometric repair, its alternate RandomLevelV213 implementation, interval-target local repair, exact perfect-tree target leaf promotion, and the existing stored-priority treap with 32-bit priorities and key tie breaking.
  • The two geometric implementations match on all operation/shape metrics in 105 paired completed trials; mismatches: 0. Their curves can overlap. The alternate additionally records the sampled move count in an insertion annotation, which is not one of the reported metrics.
  • 3 seeds per group through 65,536 keys; one seed above that size. Inputs are fixed per size and shared across strategies. Python balancing streams are paired; C++ uses an independent PRNG stream. Single large trials give no uncertainty estimate.
  • Root depth is zero. Mean depth averages all nodes in the final tree. Rotations and random bits are totals divided by inserted keys. Maximum final height is the greatest final depth across all completed seeds in that group.
  • Height, mean-depth and random-bit charts include a dashed gray c·log₂(n) guide. For each chart, c is the largest value/log₂(n) ratio at each implementation's last completed point, with a minimum of 1. The legend states c. This descriptive endpoint scaling is not a proven bound; random bits per key can remain constant even though the guide grows.
  • Every completed tree passes BST order, parent-pointer, cycle and full-key-set checks. Stored treap depths also match an independently reconstructed Cartesian tree. Validation is included in the process memory cap and deadline.
  • Python trials run concurrently in isolated processes; the native extension runs sequentially. Cross-language runtime comparisons are omitted. Memory limits and wall deadlines include instrumentation and validation overhead. Raw outcomes and missing measurements are retained, never treated as zeros.
  • The worker source was copied before running and its SHA-256 checksums recorded. Source snapshot: the parent run directory's source folder. No logarithmic-height guarantee or general performance claim follows from these finite samples.

C++ geometric repair · native benchmark extension

The five Python implementations above retain their original measurements. C++ adds 126 completed trials using the same seven input generators, input seeds, size schedule and rotation seed values. The combined charts include C++ as the sixth curve; the native-only SVGs below make its scale easier to inspect.

Implementation: signed 64-bit keys and three 32-bit indices in separate contiguous arrays: 20 bytes of reserved array payload per key. No priorities, heights or balance fields persist in nodes. Nodes are reserved before timing. SplitMix64 supplies buffered words, consumed one bit at a time without discarding unused bits. Rotation traces are disabled; counters stay enabled. The factory creates a fresh geometric strategy for each trial.

Comparability: capped geometric sampling and the straight/bent repair match Python under identical explicit bits, including duplicate behavior and rotation distances. Seed values drive different PRNGs (SplitMix64 vs Mersenne Twister), so these benchmark histories and shape metrics need not match exactly and are not paired random streams. Means have ±1 SE only for repeated seeds; largest final height is the maximum across seeds.

Timing and memory: native trials run sequentially in isolated Linux processes with a 768 MiB address-space cap and 360-second wall deadline. Insertion timing excludes input generation/parsing, startup, capacity reservation and validation. RSS includes input storage, tree arrays, validation and process overhead. The original parallel Python run did not record comparable times, so no speedup is inferred. Compiler: c++ (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810; CMake Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG with this GNU compiler), C++20. Full build settings are in config.json and the source archive.

Validation: every completed native tree passes iterative BST ordering, parent-link, acyclicity and reachability checks; all stored keys match their input slots. Original Python resource boundaries remain recorded; C++ size ceilings are reported independently. These finite runs establish neither logarithmic height nor constant traversal work.
